narrative:
The model predicted an 83% chance that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability is so high, the admissions system automatically rejected your law school application.

The decision was driven primarily by three factors, ranked by importance. By far the strongest influence was your LSAT score of 24. This is well below the average of 37 among students who were accepted, and it strongly pushed the prediction toward failure. Your first-year and third-year school decile rankings were the next two most important factors. Both were also below the averages of accepted students (5 versus 6 in year one, and 4 versus 5.8 in year three), each adding a moderate push toward a higher risk of failing the bar.

None of the other details in your profile, including your family income bracket, undergraduate GPA, gender, race, or plan to attend full-time, played a meaningful role in the outcome.

To improve your chances, you should focus on raising your LSAT score through targeted preparation, as this was the dominant reason for the rejection. Strengthening your academic performance in law school to move into higher deciles would also help. Once those areas improve, reapply—your profile would then look much stronger to the model.
